hysterical

/hih-STER-uh-kul/ — stress on second syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is hysterical is overwhelmed by extreme emotion, especially fear or distress, and loses control of their reactions.

The toddler grew hysterical when his balloon slipped away into the sky.

Example

When the doctor announces that the emergency surgery was a success, the patient's wife breaks down—laughing and crying at once, unable to form words—completely hysterical with relief and gratitude.

The wife is overwhelmed by emotion so extreme that she's lost control of her reactions; she's laughing and weeping at the same time, unable to compose herself. That total loss of emotional control in the face of overwhelming feeling is what hysterical means. 'Emotional' is far too mild.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

emotional: Emotional means showing strong feelings openly — tears, a shaking voice, a flushed face — while still staying in charge of yourself. Hysterical is far past that: emotion has taken over so completely that the person can no longer control their own reactions.

overwrought: Overwrought means worked up and strained until your nerves are stretched thin — upset, exhausted, and close to the edge. Hysterical is over that edge: an overwrought person is barely holding together, while a hysterical one has already lost control completely.

inconsolable: Inconsolable means so deep in grief or disappointment that no comfort helps — it measures how sad someone is. Hysterical measures control, not sadness: a person can be hysterical with joy or relief, laughing and sobbing, completely unable to manage their own reactions.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

composed: keeping your emotions firmly under control

levelheaded: staying sensible and calm under pressure

Where it sits · how completely emotion overrides control — upset → panicked → frantic → hysterical

upset vs. hysterical: Upset is far weaker than hysterical: an upset child may sniffle or pout, while a hysterical one is sobbing so hard that no one can calm them down.

panicked vs. hysterical: Panicked is weaker than hysterical; panic floods you with fear, but a hysterical person has gone past fear into a complete loss of control.

frantic vs. hysterical: Frantic comes closest to hysterical, but hysterical is stronger — a frantic person still scrambles for a solution, while a hysterical one can no longer manage their own reactions at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hyster

Root — hyster: womb (ancient doctors wrongly blamed the womb for extreme emotion) (Greek)

Suffix — -ical

Suffix — -ical: relating to, characterized by (Greek and Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Hysterical comes from Greek hystera, 'womb,' plus -ical, 'relating to.' Ancient doctors mistakenly believed uncontrollable emotion came from the womb; the science was abandoned long ago, but the word kept its meaning of being overwhelmed by emotion and losing control of your reactions.

Use the root in a new word: hysteria

Use the root in a new word: hysteria: When the fire alarm turned out to be a prank, the hallway hysteria faded quickly — but for a moment, nearly every student had been truly hysterical.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Hysterical describes someone in the grip of such extreme emotion—fear, grief, joy, relief—that they lose their composure entirely. Don't use it for ordinary worry, sadness, or excitement; save it for moments when someone completely breaks down or loses emotional control.
